title: Carbon monoxide poisoning: signs and what to do
asks: carbon monoxide what do i do
headache and dizzy in the tent with the stove on
found him passed out in the truck with the engine running
heater on in the cabin and everyone has a headache and is sleepy
is it safe to sleep in a running car
man down in closed shelter, stove burning, lips bright red, over
answer: Suspect carbon monoxide (CO) when people in a closed shelter or vehicle, or indoors with a stove, fuel-fired heater or running engine, get a headache, dizziness, confusion or drowsiness. CO cannot be seen or smelled.

Other signs: nausea, yawning, weariness, ringing in the ears, sudden collapse, unconsciousness. Lips and skin may be bright or cherry red (in dark-skinned people, a grayish tint to the lips and mouth), but do not wait for this: poisoning may occur without initial signs.
A person found unconscious in a closed shelter or vehicle may be a victim of CO poisoning.
Move the person to fresh air immediately.
Check everyone else who was in the same space: CO poisoning can affect several people at once. Anyone with signs needs fresh air too.
If the person is not breathing, give mouth-to-mouth resuscitation. Give CPR if necessary.
Seek medical aid promptly and evacuate the person to medical care.
Keep the person still and warm.
warnings: Rescuers are in danger too: large amounts of carbon monoxide can overcome a person in minutes without warning. Give the space adequate ventilation. The Army chemical-casualty manual requires breathing protection for anyone who must enter a closed area where high CO is known or suspected.
Never sleep in an idling vehicle. If you sit in one, make sure the exhaust pipe is not blocked by snow and keep the windows slightly open.
Keep shelters ventilated: they should not be airtight. A CO detector in shelters is highly recommended.
Shut the stove off when sleeping, or use a tent guard.
Use generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills outdoors only, at least 20 feet away from windows. Do not leave a car running in a garage or partly closed space.

quotes.text: CO is a poisonous gas which cannot be seen or smelled. CO binds to red blood cells more readily than oxygen so less oxygen is available to vital organs and tissues. It is contained in the exhaust from stoves and vehicles. CO can build up in closed spaces that are poorly ventilated. Early signs of CO poisoning are headache, confusion, dizziness, and drowsiness. Persons found unconscious in a closed shelter or vehicle may be victims of CO poisoning, especially if the lips and skin are bright red.

Whenever a squad stove fire, fuel-fired heater, or internal combustion engine is used indoors, there is danger of carbon monoxide poisoning. Fresh air in living and working quarters is vital. Carbon monoxide is a deadly, odorless gas that displaces oxygen in the blood stream.

Common symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning are— • Headache, dizziness, confusion, yawning, weariness, nausea, and ringing in the ears. • Bright red color on lips and skin. • Drowsiness and sudden collapse.

Headache, confusion, dizziness, excessive yawning, cherry red lips and mouth (in light-skinned individuals); grayish tint to lips and mouth (in dark-skinned individuals) and progresses to unconsciousness and death.

Carbon monoxide is insidious in its actions, and poisoning may occur without initial signs. The symptoms progress from throbbing headaches, vertigo, yawning, and poor visual acuity to the development of cherry-red mucous membranes, weakness and coma, subnormal temperature, weak pulse, and death.

Treatment. (1) Move to fresh air immediately. (2) Seek medical aid promptly. (3) Provide mouth-to-mouth resuscitation if victim is not breathing. (4) Administer 100% oxygen until the patient is symptom-free, usually about 4-5 hours.

Does anyone else from the same family or location have symptoms? Gaseous poisoning, like carbon monoxide poisoning, can cause altered mental status in multiple people. Carbon monoxide poisoning is usually seen in cold climates when people use indoor heating.
Move to fresh air and administer oxygen if available, provide cardiopulmonary resuscitation if needed and evacuate.

Adhere to the following for proper treatment of carbon monoxide poisoning: • Move the Soldier to open air. • Keep the victim still and warm. • If the Soldier is not breathing, administer mouth-to-mouth resuscitation. • Administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation, if necessary. • Immediately evacuate the Soldier to the nearest medical treatment facility. • Immediately administer oxygen, if available.
Large amounts of carbon monoxide can overcome a Soldier in minutes without warning causing him to lose consciousness and suffocate.

Adequate ventilation should be provided for all enclosed spaces where CO may be produced. Air safety in enclosed spaces for people to breathe may be tested by using standard CO indicator or detector devices. Individuals required to enter closed areas where high concentrations of CO are known or suspected to be present must be provided with respiratory protective devices.

CO poisoning can be prevented by maintaining adequate ventilation. Shelters should not be airtight. Soldiers should not remain stationary in idling vehicles for long periods. Under no circumstances should anyone sleep in an idling vehicle. Occupants of idling vehicles should ensure that exhaust pipes are not blocked by snowbanks, and the windows of the vehicle are slightly opened.

Use of a CO detector in shelters is highly recommended. These detectors can provide an early warning to occupants that CO levels are elevated and countermeasures need to be taken to reduce the risk of CO poisoning.

To prevent carbon monoxide poisoning— • Ensure that stoves and lanterns are functioning properly. • Do not let Soldiers warm themselves by engine exhaust. • Always crack the windows in vehicles when a heater is in use, and do not allow anyone to sleep in a running vehicle. • Use a tent guard or shut the stove off when sleeping.
Avoid carbon monoxide poisoning. Generators, camp stoves, or charcoal grills should always be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows. Never use a gas stovetop or oven to heat your home.
If you use your car to charge devices, do not leave the car running in a garage, partly closed space, or near a home to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning.
